reviews.title: The facts are WRONG.
reviews.text:
Some of the facts that pop up feel like those “7 foods that your doctor doesn’t want you to know about!” Where it claims horribly misconstrued myths and science pulled out of context.

One I just saw was “Eating bananas can help fight depression” 
I tapped on the “source” and the page said NOTHING of the sort. It only spoke about the importance of meditation, laughter, a sense of purpose, etc. Not even a single mention of “banana”.

So I actually looked into it: Bananas contain tryptophan and vitamin B-6 used for making serotonin, and also contains small amounts of serotonin itself, BUT none of it crosses the blood-brain barrier, and research has shown limited/inconclusive evidence. 

And this is just ONE of many “facts” I looked further into. 

So… why do I even own this app if it’s telling me “facts” that have no source, and no confirmed evidence that it’s true? 

It breaks my heart that so many people are giving this app a high review. Some of these “facts” are incorrect HEALTH facts. You’re actively hurting people into believing misinformation.

reviews.title: Love the concept, but there is room for improvement
reviews.text:
I like the idew of getting bite-sized randm facts. The app kind of feels like a healthier equivalent of scrolling through short form content facts. But heck, both share the same underlyimg issue when it comes to information; the more one tries to squeeze the information, the less context can be carriwd. It's nice that there is a more info button you can click on to dive deeper into the topic; however, by readimg more on some of the topics that were suggested, I found out how many of them are merely hinged on poorly sourced or framed articles or that the fact on the app itself is distorted relative to its original source. 

What I would very much appreciate to be added is a way for people to fact-check the facts, since there is so much opportunity for spreading distorted or plainly false knowledge. Options such as user feedback like reporting false or incorrect suggeswions should be added.

reviews.title: Inaccurate “Facts”
reviews.text: Ive found a good handful of “facts” that are not true what so ever, the most recent I discovered is “Shakespeare invented the word assassination” which is incorrect In the 12th-century Arabic term hashīshīn (plural of hashishiyy), meaning "hashish-users," (aka someone who smoked weed) The term arose during the Crusades and passed into European languages via Italian (assassino) and French, eventually becoming a general term for professional murderers and was later popularized by Shakespeare during the 15-16th century like many other words but was not invented by him. Simply doing a little research would be enough to determine what’s factual and fictional. • Edit, another false “fact” “Denver Colorado invented the cheeseburger” Infact Lionel Sternberger is generally credited with inventing the cheeseburger in 1924 (some sources say 1926) at his father's Pasadena, California, sandwich shop, "The Rite Spot". Legend says he experimentally placed a slice of American cheese on a sizzling hamburger patty. Key Historical Details The Inventor: Lionel Sternberger (16 years old at the time). The Location: The Rite Spot in Pasadena, California. The Origin Story: There are two popular, similar stories: he either did it as an experiment or was trying to cover up a burned patty. The Name: Originally called the "cheese hamburger," it was later shortened. First Trademark: While Sternberger created it first, Louis Ballast of the Humpty Dumpty Drive-In in Denver, Colorado, was awarded the first
